content: Those who are breastfeeding while also providing additional foods or fluids, such as infant formula or other breast milk substitutes, are encouraged to continue breastfeeding as much as possible. They should be supported with sensitivity and care to address any challenges they may face in feeding their child. Breastfeeding counseling during pregnancy or shortly after birth should focus on encouraging mothers and their families to establish a nurturing, caring, and responsive relationship with their infant. Feeding decisions during this time may be influenced by personal experiences, contextual factors, and external influences, with both shortand long-term consequences. Counseling aims to create a positive and loving environment where the newborn can thrive. Postnatal breastfeeding counseling further supports mothers and their families by fostering closeness through skin-to-skin contact and responsive feeding. Mothers may require additional assistance to build confidence in breastfeeding, recognize the milk ejection reflex (let-down), understand effective feeding techniques, and navigate feeding patterns and growth spurts. Parents and caregivers should have access to appropriate help when they encounter concerns about feeding, especially during the first few weeks after birth when breastfeeding is being established. This support is also crucial during significant life changes, such as a mother’s return to work or school, to help maintain breastfeeding according to individual circumstances. Counseling should be tailored to the individual needs, preferences, and values of mothers and families. If six sessions are not feasible, families should still be encouraged to attend as many as possible and engage meaningfully without stigma or judgment. The six recommended counseling sessions may occur at key time points: during pregnancy (antenatal period), immediately after birth (perinatal period, up to 2–3 days postpartum), at 1–2 weeks postpartum (neonatal period), during the first 3–4 months (early infancy), at 6 months (start of complementary feeding), and after 6 months (late infancy and early childhood). Additional sessions may be provided as needed, such as when planning a return to work or school or addressing breastfeeding challenges. Opportunities for counseling may also arise during routine child immunization visits. Face-to-face individual counseling is the preferred mode but can be complemented by telephone counseling or other technologies. The choice of counseling method may vary depending on the context. Telephone counseling and other technologies are increasingly used by health workers worldwide and can empower both end-users and counselors. These methods are particularly useful in situations where face-to-face counseling is limited or unavailable, such as during emergencies. The allocation of staff for breastfeeding counseling should be context-specific and integrated into the national healthcare system. Continuity of care is best achieved through collaboration and communication among all providers, including lay and peer counselors. Effective breastfeeding counseling requires robust training and mentoring programs for both lay and professional counselors. Careful planning and leadership are essential to develop the skills, knowledge, and confidence of counselors to support mothers in achieving their breastfeeding goals. A systems-based approach within healthcare and community settings, supported by cascade training and supervision, can enhance the effectiveness of breastfeeding counseling. Clearly defined skills, training, and referral systems for different levels of counselors are crucial. Lactation consultants and highly trained breastfeeding counselors can play a key role in training and supervision. Anticipatory breastfeeding counseling involves assessing potential and existing challenges that may impact a mother’s breastfeeding goals. This proactive approach helps reduce risks and complications, ensuring optimal breastfeeding outcomes. In difficult circumstances, positive feedback and emotional support are especially important to boost mothers’ confidence and self-efficacy in breastfeeding. Breastfeeding is a cornerstone of child health, development, and survival, particularly in areas where diarrhea, pneumonia, and undernutrition are leading causes of mortality in children under five. It also reduces the risk of overweight and obesity and protects maternal health globally. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, and continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods until at least 24 months of age or beyond. Despite the well-documented benefits of breastfeeding, global rates of exclusive breastfeeding remain low, with only 41% of infants under six months exclusively breastfed as of 2017. Continued breastfeeding at two years was reported at 45%. Efforts to improve breastfeeding rates have been modest, reflecting societal attitudes, challenges for working mothers, and insufficient national investment in breastfeeding support. Breastfeeding counseling is a critical intervention to improve breastfeeding practices and outcomes. It should be provided as a standard of care to pregnant women and mothers, both antenatally and postnatally, at appropriate frequencies, and through effective modes of delivery. Counseling should be tailored to individual needs and provided by trained professionals or lay counselors, depending on the context. Anticipatory counseling is particularly valuable in addressing potential challenges and supporting mothers in achieving their breastfeeding goals.
